Aim: To evaluate the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics (PK) of inclisiran in Japanese patients with high cardiovascular risk and elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C).

Methods: ORION-15 was a phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial. Patients with hypercholesterolemia, including heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH), were randomized to inclisiran sodium 100, 200, or 300 mg, or placebo and dosed subcutaneously on Days 1, 90, and 270. The primary endpoint was the percentage change from baseline to Day 180 to demonstrate the superiority of inclisiran vs. placebo. Patients who consented to the PK substudy had additional study procedures for blood collection and safety assessment.

Results: Overall, 312 patients (mean age, 63.6 years; male, 74.4%; baseline LDL-C, 114.0 mg/dL) were randomized. Baseline characteristics were well balanced among the groups. At Day 180, inclisiran at all doses demonstrated significant LDL-C and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) reductions (p＜0.0001 for both), which showed a dose–response relationship. The greatest reductions (LDL-C, 65.3%; PCSK9, 79.2%) were with inclisiran sodium 300 mg. At Day 180, ＞86% of the patients receiving inclisiran achieved the Japan Atherosclerosis Society 2017 lipid management targets compared to 8.9% for placebo. The mean (SD) plasma half-life for inclisiran was 6.8 (2.0)–7.6 (0.8) h. The incidence of adverse events with inclisiran was similar to that with placebo.

Conclusion: Inclisiran sodium 100, 200, and 300 mg demonstrated clinically meaningful and statistically significant LDL-C and PCSK9 reductions at Day 180, which were consistent over 12 months. Inclisiran was effective and well tolerated in Japanese patients with hypercholesterolemia, including HeFH.

According to the World Health Organization, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) is the leading cause of death worldwide 1) . In 2019, heart disease accounted for 15% of all deaths reported in Japan and the national medical expense was estimated to be 2 trillion yen (~18.6 billion US dollars) 2) .

Elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a major risk factor for the development of ASCVD 3 - 5) . In Japan, the prevalence of ASCVD and the associated healthcare burden have increased in recent years. Adoption of a westernized lifestyle combined with an aging population in Japan further increases the risk of ASCVD 6 , 7) . Global studies have demonstrated that lowering LDL-C levels is directly proportional to a reduction in cardiovascular (CV) risk 8 , 9) . LDL-C-modifying therapies reduce the risk of CV events and mortality by slowing the progression of ASCVD, thus leading to improved CV outcomes 10 , 11) .

The Japan Atherosclerosis Society (JAS) Guidelines for Prevention of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Diseases 2017/2022 recommend an LDL-C target based on an individual patient’s CV risk 12 , 13) . To reduce CV disease risk, the JAS Guidelines 2022 recommend statins as a first-line therapy to lower LDL-C and ezetimibe or proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors (PCSK9i) in case of insufficient efficacy with statins 13) . It is observed that only 25.4% of patients with high-risk secondary prevention (LDL-C goal ＜70 mg/dL), 60.6% of those with secondary prevention (LDL-C goal ＜100 mg/dL), and 65.5% of those with high-risk primary prevention (LDL-C goal ＜120 mg/dL) attain the recommended levels of LDL-C 14) . Goal attainment rates are even lower in patients with familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). The results from an observational study involving patients with FH from Japan reported that only 12.3% of patients without coronary artery disease (CAD) attained LDL-C levels of ＜100 mg/dL and only 1.8% patients with CAD achieved target levels of ＜70 mg/dL 15) . Consequently, the LDL-C goal attainment rate in Japan is far from optimal and ~30% of high-risk patients fail to adhere to the prescribed lipid-modifying therapies (LMTs), including combination therapies 16 , 17) . This could be explained by the existing clinical inertia observed in the management of ASCVD. Adjunct oral therapies like ezetimibe and bempedoic acid, as well as injectable therapies like antiPCSK9 monoclonal antibodies, have been reported to have less than ideal adherence rates. This underscores the necessity for the development of convenient and safe LMTs with improved adherence 18) . Long-term persistence and adherence to LMTs alongside administration guidance and pharmacist intervention are essential for maximizing the clinical effectiveness for patients with hypercholesterolemia 17) .

Inclisiran is a first-in-class small-interfering ribonucleic acid (siRNA) therapy approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and approved in over 80 countries for the treatment of adults with heterozygous FH (HeFH) or primary hyperlipidemia who require additional lowering of LDL-C, as an adjunct to diet and statin therapy 19 , 20) . Data from pivotal trials with inclisiran have shown that twice-yearly inclisiran sodium 300 mg effectively prevents hepatic PCSK9 production, resulting in consistent and long-term LDL-C reduction 21 - 26) .

Aim

ORION-15 (NCT04666298) is the first study to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and pharmacokinetics (PK) of inclisiran in Japanese patients with high CV risk (hypercholesterolemia, including HeFH) and elevated LDL-C. The primary objective of the study was to demonstrate the superiority of inclisiran in reducing LDL-C levels at different doses (inclisiran sodium 100, 200, and 300 mg) compared to placebo at Day 180.

MethodsStudy Design and Patients

ORION-15 is a phase 2, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study comprising a screening period of up to 14 days and a 12-month double-blinded treatment period. The study design also included a PK substudy ( Fig.1 ) . It was conducted across 42 study sites in Japan from January 2021 to October 2022 (Supplementary Appendix 1). The study was conducted in accordance with the trial protocol, Principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and the International Council for Harmonization Good Clinical Practice Guideline and was approved by the institutional review boards of each facility. Written informed consent was obtained from each patient before any study-specific procedure was performed.

n, number of patients.

Among the 32 patients enrolled in the PK substudy, data from 24 patients from the inclisiran treatment groups (eight from each group) were analyzed for PK results.

This study included adult Japanese patients (≥ 20 years of age) with a history of CAD or categorized as high risk (diabetes, chronic kidney disease, noncardiogenic cerebral infarction, peripheral arterial disease, or a combination of other risk factors and categorized in “high risk” as assessed by the Suita Score) by the JAS 2017 Guidelines or with HeFH and LDL-C levels higher than the target value defined by JAS 2017 12) . Patients on statins were required to receive a maximally tolerated dose, whereas those not receiving statins were required to have documented evidence of intolerance to at least one statin. Patients were excluded if they were diagnosed with homozygous FH, were treated within 90 days of screening with monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) directed toward PCSK9, or had any major adverse CV event within 3 months prior to randomization. Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are provided in Supplementary Appendix 2.

Eligible patients who consented to the PK substudy signed the separate, corresponding informed consent form before enrollment.

Randomization and Masking

Randomization was stratified by LDL-C at the screening visit (≥ 130 or ＜130 mg/dL), use of statins or other LMTs at baseline, and PK substudy participation. The randomization ratio was 1:1:1:1 if patients participated in the PK substudy. Otherwise, the ratio was 1:2:2:1 for the inclisiran sodium 100, 200, or 300 mg, and placebo groups. Randomization was conducted via an automated interactive response technology.

Patients, investigators, site staff, and the clinical trial team were blinded to the treatment allocation. Any laboratory results for lipid, lipoprotein, and PCSK9 after the first administration of the study drug were blinded for patients, site staff, and the clinical trial team. Specific sponsor members (except for blinded monitors) and other parties (as needed) were unblinded after the primary analysis database lock at Day 180 for the planned regulatory submission in Japan, and patients, investigator staff, persons performing the assessments, and sponsor-blinded monitors remained blinded until the final database lock at Day 360.

Procedures, Treatment Compliance, and Study Duration

Inclisiran sodium 100, 200, or 300 mg (equivalent to 94.5, 189, or 284 mg inclisiran, respectively) and placebo were administered as a subcutaneous injection on Days 1, 90, and 270. Study treatment was administered at the study site by qualified personnel. ORION-15 started with the PK substudy, where patients were closely monitored for an additional safety assessment. Patient samples were collected on Day 1, Day 2, Day 3, Day 5, and Day 8. Once the first 12 participants completed Day 8 and tolerability was favorable, the enrollment of other patients was started. Patients also had visits on Days 14, 30, 60, 104, 120, 150, 180, 210, 300, and 360 for efficacy measurements and safety assessments.

All patients were required to remain on their background LMT until Day 180. After Day 180, investigators were notified by the central laboratory in case an LDL-C value had increased by more than 50% or 30 mg/dL compared with the value at baseline. LMTs could be changed after Day 180. mAbs for PCSK9 and LDL-C apheresis treatment were prohibited throughout the study period.

The expected duration of patients’ involvement in the study was ~374 days, including the screening period and the follow-up period up to Day 360.

Outcomes

The primary endpoint of the ORION-15 trial was the percentage change in LDL-C from baseline at Day 180. The key secondary endpoints included the percentage change in PCSK9 and absolute change in LDL-C at Day 180 from baseline. Other secondary endpoints included the proportion of patients at Day 180 who attained the lipid control target prespecified by the JAS 2017 12) (LDL-C ＜70 mg/dL: patients with a history of CAD with additional risk factors such as FH, acute coronary syndrome, or diabetes complicated by other risk factors like noncardiogenic cerebral infarction, peripheral artery disease (PAD), chronic kidney disease, metabolic syndrome, overlap of major risk factors, and smoking; LDL-C ＜100 mg/dL: patients with a history of CAD without additional risk factors or patients with FH without a CAD history; and LDL-C ＜120 mg/dL: patients categorized as high risk) and JAS 2022 13) Guidelines (LDL-C ＜70 mg/dL: patients with a history of CAD or atherothrombotic cerebral infarction with additional risk factors such as acute coronary syndrome, FH, diabetes, and CAD complicated by atherothrombotic cerebral infarction; serum LDL-C ＜100 mg/dL: patients with a history of CAD or atherothrombotic cerebral infarction without additional risk factors, patients with FH without a CAD or atherothrombotic cerebral infarction history, and patients without CAD or atherothrombotic cerebral infarction with diabetes complicated by other risk factors such as PAD, microangiopathy, and smoking; and serum LDL-C ＜120 mg/dL: patients categorized as high risk by the JAS 2022 Guideline, i.e., those with diabetes, CKD, PAD, or a combination of other risk factors and categorized in “high risk” as assessed by the Hisayama-cho Score; attainment of the JAS 2022 lipid control target was as a posthoc analysis of the study); the number of patients reaching on-treatment LDL-C levels of ＜25, ＜50, ＜70, and ＜100 mg/dL up to Day 180; the proportion of patients with ≥ 50% LDL-C reduction from baseline up to Day 180; the percentage change in LDL-C, PCSK9, other lipids, lipoproteins, and apolipoproteins from baseline up to Day 180; the incidence and severity of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) and their association with the study drug; and measurement of antidrug antibodies (ADAs) at baseline and at Days 30, 90, 180, 270, and 360. The exploratory endpoints included the changes from baseline in LDL-C, PCSK9, and other lipids after Day 180 and up to Day 360, as well as responder analysis (the number of patients reaching LDL-C levels of ＜25, ＜50, ＜70, and ＜100 mg/dL and reaching the lipid control target prespecified by JAS 2017 12) and JAS 2022 13) , and the proportion of patients with ≥ 50% LDL-C reduction) from baseline after Day 180 up to Day 360. All efficacy parameters were laboratory assessments analyzed at a central laboratory. A full description of the methods used to measure prespecified laboratory parameters is available in Supplementary Appendix 3 22 , 23 , 27) . The PK assessments included the maximum plasma concentration (Cmax), time to reach the maximum plasma concentration, apparent terminal elimination half-life, area under curve (AUC)0–24h, AUC0–48h, AUCinf, volume of distribution based on the terminal phase, and systemic clearance.

Sample Size Calculation

Assuming a within-treatment-group standard deviation (SD) of 20% for the percentage change from baseline in LDL-C, a sample size of 308 patients was determined to provide ＞90% power for a between-treatment difference of 30% at a one-sided significance level of 0.025.

Approximately 8 patients from each treatment group (for a total of approximately 32 patients) were planned to be enrolled in a PK substudy. The PK sample size was not based on a statistical assessment. The number of patients per treatment group was considered sufficient for PK evaluation.

Statistical Analysis

The full analysis set (FAS) comprised all patients randomized to the study, with the exception of those misrandomized patients who did not receive the study drug. The primary and secondary efficacy endpoints were analyzed for the FAS. Mixed models for repeated measures analysis was used for the primary endpoint and key secondary endpoints, based on which the adjusted mean and 95% confidence interval (CI) for the percentage changes within each treatment, the adjusted mean differences and 95% CIs for between-treatment (inclisiran groups vs. placebo), and p-values are reported. Dunnett’s test was used to control the overall type 1 error at one-sided alpha of 0.025. Other efficacy endpoints were analyzed separately using frequencies and percentages by visit and treatment group. Exploratory endpoints were descriptively summarized over time and at Day 360.

Patients who received at least one dose of the study treatment were included in the safety analysis (safety set). Safety analyses are descriptive and are reported as counts and proportions (n and %). The Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 25.1 was used for the coding of the adverse events (AEs). ADA evaluations, including ADA findings, were summarized by visit and treatment group. The population for the PK analyses (PK set) included patients who received inclisiran and had measurable inclisiran concentrations. The plasma PK parameters for the PK set were summarized by treatment group using descriptive statistics (N, arithmetic mean, geometric mean, SD, median, CV%, geometric CV%, minimum, and maximum) as appropriate.

Role of the Funding Source

The ORION-15 trial was funded by Novartis. Data analyses were performed by Novartis personnel in accordance with the statistical analysis plan prepared by a qualified statistician.

Results

The first patient visit for the ORION-15 study occurred on January 29, 2021, and the last patient visit was on October 19, 2022. A total of 312 patients with hypercholesterolemia, including HeFH, were randomized following an up to 14-day screening period (55 patients in the inclisiran sodium 100 mg group, 101 patients in the 200 mg group, 99 patients in the 300 mg group, and 57 patients in the placebo group). In total, 97.8% of the patients completed the study period. Overall, seven patients discontinued the study. The primary reason for discontinuation was individual patient decision (1%), which was not related to the study treatment. The median duration of treatment exposure over the follow-up duration of 360 days was 357 days in all of the inclisiran groups and 358 days in the placebo group. Patient disposition is shown in Supplementary Fig.1 . A total of 32 patients (8 from each of the treatment groups) who consented were enrolled in the PK substudy. For the PK results, data from 24 patients who received inclisiran were analyzed.

The baseline and clinical characteristics of the patients were generally comparable across all treatment groups ( Table 1 ) . Overall, the mean (SD) age of the patients was 63.6 (10.5) years. All patients were Japanese, and the proportion of males was higher than that of females (74.4%). Most of the patients had a history of CAD (70.2%), and approximately half of the patients (55.1%) had diabetes mellitus. The proportion of patients reported to have HeFH was 18.3%. The mean baseline LDL-C (SD) was 114.0 (35.72) mg/dL and the mean baseline PCSK9 (SD) was 412.7 (115.95) ng/mL in the total patient population. At baseline, 96.2% of the patients received LMT and a total of 89.4% received statins. The proportion of patients who received ezetimibe was 40.7%. None of the patients started a new LMT or changed therapy after baseline until Day 180. A total of eight patients (one patient in the inclisiran sodium 200 mg group, four patients in the inclisiran sodium 300 mg group, and three patients in the placebo group) newly started or changed LMT after Day 180.

At Day 180, inclisiran sodium 100, 200, and 300 mg demonstrated significant reductions in LDL-C. The primary endpoints of the placebo-adjusted percentage change in LDL-C from baseline to Day 180 were −56.6% (95% CI: −64.2%, −49.0%; p＜0.0001), −60.9% (95% CI: −67.6%, −54.3%; p＜0.0001), and −65.3% (95% CI: −72.0%, −58.6%; p＜0.0001) for inclisiran sodium 100, 200, and 300 mg, respectively ( Supplementary Table 1 ) . The efficacy of inclisiran was consistent across the subgroups analyzed ( Supplementary Fig.2 ) . The LDL-C reductions were observed from Day 14 and maintained over the entire study duration of approximately 12 months. The response showed dose dependency, and the greatest percentage reduction in LDL-C was observed in the 300 mg dose of inclisiran at any visit up to Day 360 ( Fig.2 ) . The variability in the percentage change in LDL-C from baseline to Day 180 among patients is presented in a waterfall plot ( Supplementary Fig.3 ) .

The placebo-adjusted percentage changes in PCSK9 from baseline to Day 180 were −66.3% (95% CI: −72.6%, −60.1%; p＜0.0001), −73.9% (95% CI: −79.3%, −68.4%; p＜0.0001), and −79.2% (95% CI: −84.8%, −73.7%; p＜0.0001) for inclisiran sodium 100, 200, and 300 mg, respectively ( Supplementary Table 2 ) . PCSK9 reductions were observed from Day 14 and maintained over the entire study duration of approximately 12 months, which showed a dose–response relationship ( Fig.3 ) . The placebo-adjusted absolute changes in LDL-C from baseline at Day 180 were −62.5 mg/dL (95% CI: −71.5, −53.4; p＜0.0001), −67.1 mg/dL (95% CI: −75.0, −59.1; p＜0.0001), and −70.9 mg/dL (95% CI: −78.9, −62.9; p＜0.0001) for inclisiran sodium 100, 200, and 300 mg, respectively ( Supplementary Table 1 ) .

Over the 1-year treatment period, the incidence of TEAEs was comparable across all treatment groups (inclisiran sodium 100 mg: 89. 1% [n=49], inclisiran sodium 200 mg: 83.2% [n=84], inclisiran sodium 300 mg: 80.8% [n=80], and placebo: 84.2% [n=48]; Table 4 ). Most events were mild in severity. Severe TEAEs were reported in three patients with inclisiran (one patient in the inclisiran sodium 200 mg group experienced rhabdomyolysis, circulatory collapse, and peripheral artery occlusion, whereas in the inclisiran sodium 300 mg group, one patient reported unstable angina, congestive cardiac failure, infection, and electrolyte imbalance, and another patient reported acute pancreatitis) and four patients with placebo, but none was considered to be related to the study treatment ( Supplementary Table 5 ). The most common TEAEs at the maximum inclisiran dose of 300 mg were pyrexia (inclisiran sodium 300 mg: 18.2%, inclisiran sodium 200 mg: 11.9%, inclisiran sodium 100 mg: 14.5%, and placebo: 12.3%), diabetes mellitus inadequate control (inclisiran sodium 300 mg: 15.2%, inclisiran sodium 200 mg: 10.9%, inclisiran sodium 100 mg: 12.7%, and placebo: 17.5%), and diabetes mellitus (inclisiran sodium 300 mg: 12.1%, inclisiran sodium 200 mg: 11.9%, inclisiran sodium 100 mg: 20.0%, and placebo: 8.8%; Supplementary Table 5 ). There were two TEAEs that led to treatment discontinuation (one patient with chronic gastritis in the inclisiran sodium 200 mg group and one patient with idiopathic urticaria in the inclisiran sodium 300 mg group), but neither of them was considered to be related to inclisiran treatment by the investigator ( Table 4 ). TEAEs related to the study drug were comparable between the treatment groups, and there was no dose-dependent increase between the treatment groups (inclisiran sodium 100 mg: 7.3%, inclisiran sodium 200 mg: 13.9%, inclisiran sodium 300 mg: 13.1%, and placebo: 10.5%; Table 4 ). The most common drug-related TEAEs were injection site reactions in all groups (inclisiran sodium 100 mg: 5.5% [n=3], inclisiran sodium 200 mg: 10.9% [n=11], inclisiran sodium 300 mg: 5.1% [n=5], and placebo: 3.5% [n=2]; Supplementary Table 6 ). Most TEAEs at the injection site were mild and transient in nature. The details of the injection site reactions are listed in Supplementary Table 7 , along with the other AEs that were of scientific and medical interest to the sponsor (AEs of special interest [AESIs]). The AESIs were injection site reactions, hepatic events, and new-onset diabetes or worsening of diabetes mellitus. The incidence of serious TEAEs (TESAEs) was comparable between all treatment arms. A total of 27 TESAEs were reported in 22 patients. None of the SAEs was considered to be treatment related ( Supplementary Table 8 ). There was one death reported due to an unknown cause in the placebo group, which was deemed not to be related to the study treatment.

Discussion

The ORION-15 study demonstrated that inclisiran sodium at 100, 200, and 300 mg doses was well tolerated and exhibited consistent and effective reductions in LDL-C levels over 12 months in Japanese patients with high CV risk and elevated LDL-C. The efficacy of inclisiran in reducing LDL-C and PCSK9 was observed in all of the inclisiran treatment groups in a dose-dependent manner.

ORION-15 is the first study to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and PK of inclisiran in Japanese patients, and the results are consistent with those of the global phase 2 and phase 3 studies ( Fig.6 ) 21 - 24) . At Day 180, inclisiran sodium 300 mg showed the largest placebo-corrected reductions in LDL-C and PCSK9 (65.3% and 79.2%, respectively) compared to inclisiran sodium 200 mg (60.9% and 73.9%, respectively) and inclisiran sodium 100 mg (56.6% and 66.3%, respectively). These reductions were consistent throughout the 12-month study for all inclisiran groups and were consistent with the results of the global inclisiran trials with twice-yearly inclisiran sodium 300 mg (after the initial and 3-month dosing), which have shown placebo-corrected LDL-C reductions of up to 52% 22 , 23) . The percentage reductions in LDL-C from baseline to Day 180 were in favor of the inclisiran groups across all subgroups, including baseline statin usage ( Supplementary Fig.2 ) . Meta-analysis from the phase 3 ORION program (ORION-9, ORION-10, and ORION-11) involving 3660 patients with FH, ASCVD, and high-risk primary prevention demonstrated a consistent placebo-corrected PCSK9 reduction of approximately 80% 27) . In this study, the clinical efficacy of inclisiran in lowering not only LDL-C and PCSK9 but also non HDL-C, apoB, and Lp(a) was observed. Furthermore, at Day 180, the levels of HDL-C and apoA1 were increased. These results are in line with those of global and long-term studies 21 - 26) . The majority of the patients in ORION-15 attained the JAS 2017 lipid modification targets at Day 180, outcomes that were much higher than those observed in the placebo group. Similar results were observed at Day 180 in the posthoc analysis for the attainment of Japanese lipid modification targets specified by the JAS 2022 Guidelines 13) .

The PK of inclisiran observed in ORION-15 was dose proportional, with a short plasma half-life of 6.8 (2.0)–7.6 (0.8) h. The mean Cmax reported with inclisiran sodium 300 mg was 607 ng/mL, and the AUCinf was 12300 ng*h/mL. At all doses, inclisiran was undetectable in plasma after 24 to 48 h. These results are in line with what has been described in the global PK studies with inclisiran 24) .

The safety profile of inclisiran reported in ORION-15 is in line with that reported in the global pivotal trials and the long-term study with inclisiran 21 - 26) . In this study, AEs at the injection site were reported as the most common drug-related TEAEs, in line with those reported in the global trials. It is worth noting that the majority of these events were mild and resolved by the end of the study period. Slightly more hepatic events were observed with inclisiran sodium 300 mg, but none was serious and there was no time correlation between the events and inclisiran administration. In addition, two of these patients had liver steatosis at baseline. No meaningful changes were observed in clinical laboratories for liver enzymes. Most diabetes TEAEs were mild in severity and there was no dose dependency observed, regardless of baseline diabetes status. The ADA-positive status in this study revealed no evidence for immunogenicity with any of the inclisiran doses. Similar safety findings for clinical immunogenicity AEs were observed in the global phase 2 and phase 3 trials, which provides reassurance regarding the safety of inclisiran 22 , 23 , 28) .

Inclisiran is a first-in-class siRNA therapy with a mechanism of action (MoA) that prevents the production of PCSK9 protein through gene silencing, subsequently leading to reduced LDL-C levels. Evolocumab and alirocumab, which are antiPCSK9 mAbs, exert a rapid onset of action by the inhibition of circulating PCSK9 within 1 day postinjection, reaching a nadir close to zero between Day 3 and Day 4, whereas inclisiran reduces total PCSK9 levels by 70% 3 days postinjection owing to its complex MoA and liver-specific prevention of PCSK9 synthesis 5 , 29 - 31) . Inclisiran has emerged as an alternative approach to antiPCSK9 mAbs, which are directed against PCSK9 and prevent its binding to the LDL receptor 32) . AntiPCSK9 mAbs are administered by subcutaneous injection biweekly or monthly, and inclisiran is administered twice yearly (after the initial and 3-month dosing) as a subcutaneous injection 19 , 20 , 33 , 34) . Therefore, it must be considered that patient adherence to 13–26 injections per year with antiPCSK9 mAbs might pose a challenge to treatment compliance 35) . The efficacy and safety of inclisiran demonstrated over ~5 years of treatment, when combined with the advantage of its infrequent dosing schedule, may provide a convenient option as an add-on LMT 26 , 36) .

Study Strength and Limitation

The results of ORION-15 confirm the clinical applicability of inclisiran for Japanese patients with high CV risk and elevated LDL-C. Longer-term efficacy and safety data (＞1 year) for inclisiran are not available for Japanese patients. The study does not demonstrate the impact of inclisiran in the reduction in CV outcomes, but this is currently being studied in the CV outcome trials ORION-4 (NCT03705234) and VICTORION-2 Prevent (NCT05030428), each enrolling ~15,000 participants 37 , 38) .

Conclusion

ORION-15 is the first study to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and PK of inclisiran in Japanese patients with high CV risk and elevated LDL-C. The results demonstrated robust and consistent reductions in LDL-C and PCSK9 levels in Japanese patients over the entire 12-month study period. The efficacy of inclisiran was observed at all doses and in a dose-dependent manner. Twice-yearly inclisiran (after the initial and 3-month dosing) was well tolerated in Japanese patients with hypercholesterolemia, including HeFH.

Appendix 3: Laboratory and Analytical Methods

All analyses were performed by Medpace Reference Laboratories (MRL) who are certified in the CDC-NHLBI Lipid Standardization Part III Program.

PCSK9 analysis was performed using Quantikine ELISA from R&D Systems according to the manufacturer’s instructions using a Tecan Sunrise reader and EDTA-plasma. Intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation were observed to be 4.7% and 5.4%. Completed patient sets were analyzed on the same plate to eliminate inter-assay variability when comparing results within a patient.

Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) was determined by both the Friedewald formula, and additionally by preparative ultracentrifugation (PUC). LDL-C methods remained the same throughout the trial, including both calibration and reagent systems. MRL does not change methods during the course of a study. Reflexive testing for LDL-C with ultracentrifugation was performed if LDL-C was ＜40 mg/dl or triglycerides (TG) was greater than 400 mg/dl. Baseline samples were not reanalyzed if LDL-C fell below 40 mg/dl during the trial.

Analytical Methods (Includes All Methods Required to Derive LDL Cholesterol by Friedewald and PUC)

Analysis of total cholesterol (TC) and TG were by enzymatic methods on a Beckman Coulter AU Series automatic analyzer with in-house developed serum calibrators directly traceable to CDC-NHLBI reference procedures. (Ref: Myers GL, Cooper GR, et al: The Centers for Disease Control-National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute Lipid Standardization Program: An approach to accurate and precise lipid measurements. HDL cholesterol was performed by precipitation with 50 kDa dextran sulfate with magnesium ions (MgCl2), followed by analysis of the supernatant for cholesterol by enzymatic methods on a Beckman Coulter AU Series automatic analyzer with in-house developed serum calibrators directly traceable to CDC-NHLBI reference procedures (same methodology as TC).

PUC was performed using the method outlined in the Lipid Research Clinics methods manual. (Ref: US Department of Health and Human Services. Manual of laboratory operations: lipid and lipoprotein analysis (revised). Washington, DC: US Government Printing Office; 1982. Report No.: (NIH) 75-67815).

Serum or plasma was overlaid with normal saline (density 1.006 g/mL) and centrifuged (Beckman Ultracentrifuge Model # L-90K and rotor, Type 50.4) at 40,000 rpm for 18–22 hours at 10℃ to separate very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) in the supernatant (‘top’ fraction) from LDL and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) in the infranatant or ‘bottom’ fraction. The cholesterol concentration of the infranatant was measured. All apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins, VLDL, LDL, and lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)], were precipitated from serum using 50 kDa dextran sulfate with magnesium ions (MgCl2), and the cholesterol in the remaining HDL fraction was measured. The HDL cholesterol concentration was subtracted from the infranatant cholesterol to provide the PUC LDL cholesterol value.

Calculated LDL cholesterol was derived from the Friedewald formula where:

LDL cholesterol=TC−(HDL cholesterol＋TG/5)

[for mmol/L, LDL cholesterol=TC−HDL cholesterol−(TG/2.2)].

Lp(a): MRL uses an automated monoclonal antibody immunoturbidometric ‘isoformindependent’ method, meaning independent of Lp(a) particle size. The calibrators for this kit are referenced against WHO SRM 2B. Since there is significant heterogeneity in Lp(a) particles, the assay used should be insensitive to the size of apo(a)─the protein bound to apo B-100. Results are reported in nmol/L of Lp(a) protein, rather than mass units, due to the varying mass ratio of apo(a) to apoB in different sized Lp(a) particles. The Polymedco Lp(a) method in use at MRL is analyzed on a Beckman Coulter AU Series analyzer, and is referenced to an International Reference Material (SRM 2B) developed by the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry (IFCC), and approved by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI). This allows accurate measurement of Lp(a) levels irrespective of isoform size.

Apolipoproteins AI and B were measured using nephelometric methodology on a Siemens BNII analyzer.
